name: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask
title: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask
answer: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask is a family communication tool built on the idea that parents have a right to understand how their children's school uses AI. The five questions cover approved tools, signed data agreements, human decision making, teaching students to use AI well, and how to raise concerns. A school that can answer them clearly shows accountability and builds trust with families.

sections.body: The idea is that parents should not have to guess how AI affects their child at school. It gives families five concrete questions, and it gives schools a standard for the answers they should be able to provide. The questions address which tools touch a child's information, whether the school has signed agreements with the companies, who makes decisions about a child, how children are taught to use AI well, and what a parent can do with a concern. A school that cannot answer clearly has more work to do, and board members can use the same questions to check on a district. This solves the problem of vague or missing communication about AI, which leaves families without a way to understand or question school practice.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a school keeps a public list of approved AI tools and can show which ones a particular child uses. It can confirm that every tool that handles student data is covered by a signed agreement limiting how that data is used. It can state that people, not machines, make every important decision about a child and can describe its human review rule. It can explain its AI use levels and how teachers check that students are learning rather than just finishing tasks. It also names a contact person for concerns, explains how to request a child's records, and describes how to opt out where options exist, with no grade band variations given in the text.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book presents this idea as a practical checklist in Figure 14.5 rather than as a research finding. It says a school that cannot answer the five questions clearly has more work to do, and it notes that board members can use the same questions to check on their district. No study, statistic, or formal evidence label is given in the supplied text. This idea therefore rests on practice and on the judgment that clear answers build trust, not on research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that clear answers depend on the school actually having the practices in place, not just the words to describe them. The text keeps important decisions with people, not machines, and requires a human review rule for decisions about a child. Parents should never have to guess whom to call, so a named contact, a way to request records, and an opt out process where options exist are part of the guardrails. If a school cannot answer the five questions clearly, the text says it has more work to do. The decisions about a child's education and about how concerns are handled stay with people, and this description is practice rather than legal advice.
